chunks: And the Sheikh, may God have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far b. Muhammad, from Muhammad b. Ya'qub, from Muhammad b. Yahya, from Ahmad b. Muhammad, from 'Uthman b. 'Isa, from Sama'a, who said:

I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about a water jar in which a beetle was found dead. He said: Throw it out and perform wudu from it [the water]. And if it was a scorpion, then pour out the water and perform wudu from other water.

And [I also asked] about a man who has two vessels containing water, into one of which an impurity fell and he does not know which one it is, and he has no other water available. He said: He should pour both out and perform tayammum.

key_terms.جَرَّةٍ: an earthen water jar for storing water; subject of the first ruling
key_terms.خُنْفَسَاءُ: a dung/black beetle; an insect lacking flowing blood whose carcass does not render water impure (najis) under Shia fiqh
key_terms.عَقْرَبًا: a scorpion; its carcass renders water impure, requiring disposal
key_terms.قَذَرٌ: ritual impurity; any najis substance that contaminates water
key_terms.يَتَيَمَّمُ: to perform tayammum (dry ablution with clean earth) as a substitute when water is unavailable or entirely impure

ai.seo_question: What is Imam al-Sadiq's ruling on water purity when a dead beetle or scorpion is found in a jar, and what should a man do if he cannot identify which of two water vessels is impure?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) issues two rulings on water purity (taharah): a dead beetle does not render small water (mā' qalīl) impure — it is removed and wudu may be performed — whereas a dead scorpion does, requiring the water to be discarded. When a man's two vessels are both suspect due to unidentifiable impurity, and no alternative water exists, he must discard both and resort to tayammum. These rulings reflect the Shia jurisprudential principle that certainty of najasah triggers prohibition, while mere doubt in the absence of alternatives is resolved by tayammum.
